mao.1.tier_reason: Core: fits the opening of any argument, report or email, and decides whether the reader keeps going.
mao.1.why: When readers open a piece, the first thing they want to know is what it is for. A first sentence that answers this gives them a target, so every later paragraph has somewhere to land. Skipping the preamble also shows the writer has thought it through. Opening with a question adds one more effect: the reader starts answering it in their head.
mao.1.example:
> 谁是我们的敌人？谁是我们的朋友？这个问题是革命的首要问题。（《中国社会各阶级的分析》）

*Gloss:* Who are our enemies? Who are our friends? This is the first question of the revolution. (*Analysis of the Classes in Chinese Society*)
mao.1.breakdown:
- Two questions side by side: the question the whole piece answers is laid out in one breath.
- “The first question”: says at once why it is worth reading.
- Not a word of background: the first sentence is the subject itself.
mao.1.overdo:
> With the continuous development of the times and profound changes in society, meetings, as an important form of organizational communication, are attracting more and more attention.

The problem is three layers of filler: after a whole sentence you still do not know what the piece is about, and the subject has not appeared.
mao.1.when_not:
- Narrative or lyrical writing that needs to set a scene first.
- When the subject is sensitive for the reader and a blunt opening may push them away.
mao.1.exercise: Take something you wrote recently, delete the first paragraph, and rewrite the opening as a question.
mao.1.check: Reading only the first sentence, can someone say what problem the piece sets out to solve?
mao.1.adjacent:
- mao.10 Friendly Call (head and tail: ask at the start, land on something doable at the end)
- mao.3 Numbered Points (once the problem is stated, numbered points often follow)

mao.2.tier_reason: Common: useful for analyzing groups, problems and options, but you need to find a single criterion.
mao.2.why: A tangle of phenomena, once sorted, has boxes. Readers can place things and feel they now see how it works. One consistent criterion with clear borders between classes makes the analysis look grounded; a stance attached to each class tells readers how to treat it.
mao.2.example:
> *Paraphrase:* *Analysis of the Classes in Chinese Society* lists the classes of society one by one by economic position, describing each one's situation and its attitude to the revolution.
>
> *Demonstration:* People at meetings come in roughly three kinds: those who come to speak, those who come to listen, and those who come to sit.
mao.2.breakdown:
- One criterion only: what you came to the meeting to do.
- “Those who come to sit”: the third class is unexpected and points to the problem.
- The three classes do not overlap: each person falls into one box.
mao.2.overdo:
> Young people today fall into the following types: the lying-flat type, the rat-race type, the Zen type, those born after 1995, the socially anxious type, and slash careerists.

The problem is a muddled criterion: personality, attitude and age are mixed, the classes overlap, and the sorting sorts nothing.
mao.2.when_not:
- When the subject has only one or two cases; forced classes look like padding.
- When giving feedback to one specific person; classes can feel like labels.
mao.2.exercise: Sort the people in your office into three classes by how they reply to messages, one sentence each, and check whether anyone falls into two.
mao.2.check: Can you name the criterion, and does each item belong to exactly one class?
mao.2.adjacent:
- mao.3 Numbered Points (classifying cuts up the subject; numbering lines up problems or remedies)
- mao.6 Negative Example (one class can be expanded into a type portrait)

mao.3.tier_reason: Core: works in reports, proposals and arguments alike, and best helps readers grasp the structure.
mao.3.why: Numbers give readers a map: how many points there are and which one they are on. A short line at the head of each point works like a subheading and sticks at a glance; by the time it is expanded, readers already know what to expect. Stating the count up front is also a promise: say three, deliver three.
mao.3.example:
> *Paraphrase:* *Oppose Stereotyped Party Writing* first says such writing has many faults, then lists eight of them one by one, each opening with a short phrase before it is expanded.
>
> *Demonstration:* Meetings go badly for three reasons. First, no agenda. Second, discussion without decision. Third, decision without action.
mao.3.breakdown:
- “Three reasons”: the total comes first, so readers know the size.
- “No agenda”, “discussion without decision”, “decision without action”: each short enough to say in one breath.
- The order follows the meeting itself: before, during, after. The sequence is the logic.
mao.3.overdo:
> First, we must raise awareness. Second, we must strengthen leadership, improve mechanisms, tighten assessment, implement firmly, and build long-term mechanisms.

The problem is uneven points: the first is empty, the second crams in five things, and the numbers are decoration.
mao.3.when_not:
- With only one point, do not force a “first”.
- In lyrical or narrative writing, numbers break the flow.
mao.3.exercise: Write “why I always procrastinate” as three points, none longer than eight words.
mao.3.check: Can the first sentence of each point stand alone as a subheading, and do the points carry similar weight?
mao.3.adjacent:
- mao.2 Classify and Analyze (classifying cuts the subject; numbering lines up points)
- mao.9 Short Parallels (numbering is structure; parallelism is sentence shape)

mao.4.tier_reason: Common: usable in any argument, but the analogy must fit the point and be restrained on formal occasions.
mao.4.why: Abstract reasoning makes readers work; everyday life they already understand. Explaining “judgment” through cooking lets readers borrow experience they have, so they get it at once and remember it. A saying also carries the weight of “that is what everyone says”, so the point does not feel forced on them by the writer.
mao.4.example:
> *Paraphrase:* *Oppose Stereotyped Party Writing* uses the doctor's “prescribe for the illness” to show why problems must be analyzed; *The Foolish Old Man Who Removed the Mountains* borrows an ancient fable to make the case for persistence.
>
> *Demonstration:* A meeting is like stir-frying: too little heat and the dish is raw, too much and it burns.
mao.4.breakdown:
- “Stir-frying”: everyone has done it; no barrier to entry.
- “Raw” and “burnt”: both extremes are wrong, matching meetings that are too short and too long.
- “Heat” is never explained: readers map it themselves.
mao.4.overdo:
> Life is like a marathon, and also like a cup of coffee, and even more like a book; only by savoring it slowly can we understand its sweetness and bitterness.

The problem is piled-up analogies cut loose from the point: three unrelated images ending in an empty “savoring”.
mao.4.when_not:
- Serious accident reports or memorial writing, where a folk saying reads as flippant.
- When the analogy needs a long explanation to work; say it plainly instead.
mao.4.exercise: Explain “why study needs review” with one kitchen analogy, in one sentence.
mao.4.check: Remove the analogy: is the point unchanged? Do both ends of the analogy match one to one?
mao.4.adjacent:
- mao.7 Positive Model (the analogy uses a comparison; the model uses a real case as evidence)
- mao.9 Short Parallels (sayings often close with a parallel run)

mao.5.tier_reason: Signature: dialectical analysis is the hallmark of this style; beginners tend to turn it into splitting the difference.
mao.5.why: Show only one side and readers think you missed the other; show both and they feel it is fair and keep listening. The key is the second half: naming the principal side gives the piece a judgment and a direction instead of a muddle.
mao.5.example:
> *Paraphrase:* *On Contradiction* argues that things contain principal and secondary contradictions, and each contradiction has a principal and a secondary aspect; analysis must grasp the principal one.
>
> *Demonstration:* Having many meetings has downsides and upsides. People meet, information flows; that is the good side. But the main problem is that the meeting ends and nothing gets done.
mao.5.breakdown:
- “Downsides and upsides”: both sides are laid out first.
- “That is the good side”: a sincere concession, not a formality.
- “But the main problem is”: the judgment lands here and sets the direction for the whole piece.
mao.5.overdo:
> Overtime has both positive and negative aspects; we must view it dialectically, neither rejecting it wholesale nor accepting it wholesale.

The problem is two sides and no verdict: “view it dialectically” becomes a shield for not taking a position.
mao.5.when_not:
- Questions of principle, where right and wrong are clear; hunting for a “good side” is a mistake.
- When readers want steps to follow, not analysis.
mao.5.exercise: Write two sentences on “scrolling short videos”: the first grants one benefit, the second names the main problem.
mao.5.check: After reading, can you say clearly which side the writer thinks is principal?
mao.5.adjacent:
- mao.8 Anticipated Objection (two sides is weighing both yourself; the objection speaks for the other party)
- mao.2 Classify and Analyze (classifying makes several boxes; two sides makes two)

mao.6.tier_reason: Common: good for criticizing a way of working or pointing out a problem, but never insinuate a real person.
mao.6.why: “Formalism” in general leaves readers cold. Sketch one concrete practice and they immediately recall the version they have seen, and smile or blush. A nickname spreads easily and becomes shorthand. Naming no one means readers cannot pass it off onto someone else; they can only check themselves.
mao.6.example:
> *Paraphrase:* *Reform Our Study* sketches a way of working that does no investigation and only talks theory, describing the practice without naming anyone.
>
> *Demonstration:* There is a kind of “relay man”: back from a meeting, he reads out what the boss said, and that counts as implementing it.
mao.6.breakdown:
- “Relay man”: a short nickname, easy to remember and repeat.
- “Reads out”: one concrete action, easy to picture.
- “That counts as implementing it”: the word “counts” carries the irony; no abuse needed.
mao.6.overdo:
> Certain people are seriously divorced from reality, inflated in style, rigid in thinking, inactive or reckless, and have caused extremely bad effects on the work.

The problem is all verdict and no portrait: a string of pejoratives, and not one concrete practice for readers to see.
mao.6.when_not:
- When a specific colleague could be recognized; it hurts and causes trouble.
- When the piece aims to encourage; wall-to-wall negatives deflate it.
mao.6.exercise: Give the habit of “only looking at your phone in meetings” a short nickname and write its typical action in one sentence.
mao.6.check: Did you describe the practice and not the person, and can readers picture a concrete scene from that sentence?
mao.6.adjacent:
- mao.7 Positive Model (same family; one negative and one positive often appear as a pair)
- mao.2 Classify and Analyze (a negative example can be one of the classes)

mao.7.tier_reason: Common: useful for showing how something should be done, but it must be real and specific, never invented.
mao.7.why: However right the argument, readers wonder whether it can actually be done. A real example close at hand answers that: someone did it, and you can see how. A concrete method can be copied, which moves people more than a slogan.
mao.7.example:
> *Paraphrase:* *In Memory of Norman Bethune* shows a spirit through one man's deeds; *Serve the People* starts from an ordinary soldier.
>
> *Demonstration:* An older colleague in our section writes the three items to be discussed on a sheet of paper before every meeting, goes through them one by one, and always finishes in twenty minutes.
mao.7.breakdown:
- “An older colleague in our section”: someone nearby, not a distant hero.
- “On a sheet of paper”, “one by one”: a concrete method you can copy.
- “Always finishes in twenty minutes”: the result, proof that it works.
mao.7.overdo:
> For decades he has been diligent and conscientious, uncomplaining and selfless, never caring about personal gain, a shining example for us all.

The problem is a perfect person: all virtue adjectives and not one concrete deed, so readers neither believe it nor can learn from it.
mao.7.when_not:
- When you have no real example; better none than an invented life story.
- When readers lack the model's conditions entirely; what they cannot copy only distances them.
mao.7.exercise: Write how someone you know does one small thing well, in two sentences: one for the method, one for the result.
mao.7.check: After reading, could someone carry out the same action?
mao.7.adjacent:
- mao.6 Negative Example (one positive, one negative)
- mao.4 Folk Analogy (the model uses a real case; the analogy uses a comparison)

mao.8.tier_reason: Core: every persuasive piece needs it; it decides whether readers who disagree come away convinced.
mao.8.why: A reader with an unspoken doubt keeps resisting. Say the doubt for them and they feel understood and lower their guard; granting what is reasonable looks fair, so they are more willing to hear the answer. Once the doubt is dealt with early, the rest of the piece has no hidden rocks.
mao.8.example:
> *Paraphrase:* *Oppose Stereotyped Party Writing* and *Serve the People* both contain passages that raise a likely doubt and then answer it.
>
> *Demonstration:* Some will say that short meetings leave some things unclear. There is something in that. But what cannot be made clear is usually what was not thought through before the meeting.
mao.8.breakdown:
- “Some will say”: speaking for the other side, with a real and common objection.
- “There is something in that”: conceding first lowers the temperature in a few words.
- “Not thought through before the meeting”: the answer does not deny the objection; it moves the problem somewhere more basic.
mao.8.overdo:
> Some may say meetings are completely useless and no one should hold them at all. This view is obviously extremely absurd.

The problem is a straw man: make the objection stupid and kick it away, and those who disagree only dig in.
mao.8.when_not:
- When readers already agree; inventing opposition is redundant.
- When you cannot think of a decent objection; do not build a fake target.
mao.8.exercise: On “getting up an hour earlier every day”, write the strongest objection, grant it, then answer in one sentence.
mao.8.check: Would someone who holds the objection read your version and think, “Yes, that is exactly what I think”?
mao.8.adjacent:
- mao.5 Two Sides (same family; two sides weighs both yourself, the objection is a reply in dialogue)
- mao.1 Straight to the Point (the opening states the thesis; the objection defends it)

mao.9.tier_reason: Common: good for closing and emphasis, but overuse turns into slogan-speak.
mao.9.why: Repeated structure sets a beat for the ear, so readers follow without effort; short sentences put the force on a few key words; several in a row raise feeling and meaning together. It is best for gathering the argument into one line people remember.
mao.9.example:
> ……就是一个高尚的人，一个纯粹的人，一个有道德的人，一个脱离了低级趣味的人，一个有益于人民的人。（《纪念白求恩》）

*Gloss:* …is a noble person, a pure person, a person of moral integrity, a person above vulgar interests, a person of value to the people. (*In Memory of Norman Bethune*)
mao.9.breakdown:
- “A … person” five times: the frame stays fixed and the ear catches the beat.
- The modifiers go from short to long and back to short: the rhythm rises and falls instead of plodding.
- Placed at the end: it gathers the whole account of one man into a set of standards.
mao.9.overdo:
> We must throw ourselves into work with ever fuller enthusiasm, push forward every task with an ever more practical style, and meet new challenges with ever higher fighting spirit.

The problem is long, empty sentences: each runs twenty-odd words, swapping the nouns changes nothing, and only the sound of a slogan is left.
mao.9.when_not:
- Parallels in every paragraph tire readers and make them suspect slogans.
- When the content is not actually parallel, forcing the structure feels awkward.
mao.9.exercise: Sum up your ideal weekly meeting in three short sentences of the same shape, each no more than eight words.
mao.9.check: Is every sentence short, and does swapping the key word really change the meaning?
mao.9.adjacent:
- mao.3 Numbered Points (numbering expands the points; parallels gather them)
- mao.10 Friendly Call (parallels often lead straight into the closing call)

mao.10.tier_reason: Common: argument and mobilizing pieces need a landing point; narrative and pure analysis do not.
mao.10.why: After the reasoning, the reader's worst moment is “and then?” One concrete small thing gives them a way out: they can close the piece and act. A plain tone, like a suggestion, does not feel like an order, so they are more willing to try. A small, specific ask has a low threshold, which makes it far more likely to get done.
mao.10.example:
> *Paraphrase:* *The Foolish Old Man Who Removed the Mountains* and *Serve the People* both close on concrete, doable requests rather than abstract slogans.
>
> *Demonstration:* Next time we meet, why not start with one small thing: put the agenda in the notice, and before we break up, ask “Who is doing it, and by what day?”
mao.10.breakdown:
- “Next time we meet”: a clear time, close at hand.
- “Why not”, “one small thing”: the tone of a suggestion lowers the burden.
- “Who is doing it, and by what day?”: a line you can say as written and use immediately.
mao.10.overdo:
> Let us join hands, unite our hearts and minds, forge ahead, and together create a better tomorrow!

The problem is empty exhortation: not one thing the reader can do tomorrow, only a string of words that could end any article.
mao.10.when_not:
- When the piece exists to analyze or record, and readers need no action.
- When readers are too varied to act together; a forced call feels imposed.
mao.10.exercise: Write the ending of a short piece on staying up less late, allowing only one thing that can be done tonight.
mao.10.check: After the ending, can readers name one specific action they will take tomorrow?
mao.10.adjacent:
- mao.1 Straight to the Point (head and tail: the question and the landing point)
- mao.9 Short Parallels (the parallels build momentum, the call lands it)
